routes.description: Establish that the canonical Gospels are best connected to Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John through converging early attribution, text-specific internal features, and historically plausible forms of source use or authorized collaboration.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the attribution tradition and internal indicators jointly identify the traditional figures or their authority more plausibly than a later naming process, while accounting for anonymity, Greek literary composition, source dependence, and oral transmission.

motionBridge.description: Connect each canonical Gospel to its traditional namesake as writer, source, or authorizing authority in the sense required by the motion.

centralBridges.description: Show that the timing, distribution, consistency, and content of early testimony preserve genuine authorship information rather than a dependent later convention.
Show that salient textual features independently fit the proposed Matthean, Petrine-Markan, Lukan, and Johannine connections.
Show that differences in education and language are compatible with traditional authority through source use, assistants, or collaborative literary production.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why formally unnamed narratives or third-person narration do not sever an otherwise supported connection to traditional authors.
Explain how oral circulation, literary dependence, and selective narration can remain closely grounded in apostolic testimony.

routes.description: Establish that the canonical texts do not supply adequate identifications of Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John and that their literary characteristics and attribution history are better explained by anonymous educated authors and later church naming.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the evidence fails to connect the canonical texts to the traditional figures or their authorization, while anonymous circulation, educational mismatch, and the emergence and propagation of later names provide a coherent alternative account.

motionBridge.description: Show that neither direct composition nor authorization by the four traditional figures is adequately established for the canonical Gospels.

centralBridges.description: Show that securely identifiable traditional names arise too late or dependently to establish knowledge of original authorship.
Show that the language, education, and compositional demands of the texts conflict with authorship by the traditional Galilean disciples.
Show that first-person passages, eyewitness claims, narrative details, and conventional author labels do not identify the traditional figures.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Provide a historically coherent reason authoritative communities could assign and then preserve apostolically useful names.
Distinguish attested dictation or letter-writing assistance from independent composition of lengthy literary narratives for an illiterate authority.

sections.title: Timing, independence, and reach of external attribution
sections.rationale: The historical value of Papias, Justin, Irenaeus, and other witnesses is a principal test of whether the traditional names preserve early authorship knowledge or reflect a later dependent convention.

sections.title: Literacy, language, and mediated composition
sections.rationale: The motion turns partly on whether the traditional figures could compose the Greek narratives themselves or exercise authorship authority through assistants, sources, and collaborative production.

sections.title: Internal textual indicators of authorial identity
sections.rationale: Travel narration, eyewitness claims, disciple rosters, Petrine features, and Matthean characteristics matter insofar as they identify particular authors rather than merely remaining compatible with them.

sections.title: Anonymous circulation and the formation of Gospel names
sections.rationale: Ancient naming conventions and the proposed second-century attribution process determine whether initial anonymity is neutral or supports an alternative explanation for later unanimity.

sections.title: Source dependence, oral transmission, and apostolic proximity
sections.rationale: Synoptic borrowing, oral tradition, selective biography, and unwitnessed material bear on whether the texts remained sufficiently grounded in the named disciples or their immediate circles.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
moves.proposition: Six early witnesses from geographically diverse Christian regions agree on the traditional Gospel attributions, supporting preservation of genuine authorship information.
moves.attributionBasis: The uninterrupted opening-statement turn and first-person framing identify Michael Licona as the speaker.

response.rationale: This constructive move establishes the affirmative external-attestation case and therefore has no earlier opposing target to answer.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it directly and substantially develops a principal route bridge with multiple named witnesses and regions.

precisionFindings.rationale: The claim, witness count, geographic scope, and inferential purpose are recoverable, though independence among the witnesses remains an implicit qualification.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Diversity and agreement support the conclusion, but the strong bottom-line formulation exceeds the excerpt's treatment of witness independence and dating disputes.

charity.alternative: The geographically dispersed witnesses may repeat an already established attribution tradition rather than supply independent testimony.
charity.decisiveQualification: Geographic diversity alone does not demonstrate informational independence or access to original authorship knowledge.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The inference from early, distributed agreement to preserved information is coherent, with informational independence left as one important implicit bridge.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: It supplies a witness count, date range, and regions, but compresses source-by-source dating, independence, and alternative transmission analysis.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly cites six sources, a range of fifteen to one hundred years after the final Gospel, unanimity, and five geographic regions.

charity.decisiveQualification: The internal passages identify at most a traveling participant unless their narrative voice and the external attribution are independently established.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes the we-narrative, roughly a dozen Pauline coworkers, Luke's appearance in three letters, and unanimous external attribution.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
moves.proposition: Matthew likely shaped or authorized the surviving Greek Gospel with assistance, sources, and substantial additional material even if his earlier Semitic composition was lost.

components.text: Whether evidence for ancient literacy assistance warrants book-length independent Gospel composition under an illiterate authority.
Whether short dictated-letter practice is an adequate historical analogy for a twenty-eight-chapter literary narrative.
Whether bare compatibility with assistance supplies evidence of actual mediated authorship.

response.rationale: The reply expressly diagnoses a category difference between short formulaic dictation and autonomous narrative composition and states that the former does not warrant the latter.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the challenged analogy's failure and states the defeating consequence for the proposed collaborator warrant.

precisionFindings.rationale: Short formulaic letters, content-taking, and long narrative composition are clearly distinguished with a stable and appropriately limited conclusion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical difference claim is proportionate to the contrasted literary tasks and does not deny every possible form of collaboration.

charity.alternative: Some ancient collaborators could exercise more extensive compositional discretion than ordinary letter scribes, making Gospel-scale assistance possible.
charity.decisiveQualification: Possibility requires separate evidence because routine short-letter practice does not establish the relevant extended literary practice.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The analogy is diagnosed at the exact point of disanalogy, and the consequence for the affirmative warrant follows explicitly.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The contrast in length, formula, plot, characterization, themes, and emphasis is specific, though representative documentation is compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary secretarial-limits bridge and occupies the highest portion of that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply grants the familiar evidence its proper scope and precisely explains why it does not carry the stronger mediated-composition burden.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts short, formulaic Roman letters containing supplied content with a twenty-eight-chapter narrative involving plot, characters, themes, and emphasis.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
moves.proposition: Papias's statement that Mark recorded everything remembered from Peter is reasonably read as hyperbole, since historians and biographers selectively include source material.
moves.attributionBasis: The question is addressed to Mike, and the answer directly interprets Papias while defending Mark’s selectivity regarding material about Peter.

components.text: Whether Mark's omission of Petrine material defeats the claim that Mark substantially recorded Peter's remembered teaching.
Whether Papias's statement must be read literally as an exhaustive inventory of Peter's recollections.

response.rationale: The reply directly answers the omission challenge by interpreting everything as ordinary biographical hyperbole and invoking selective historical narration.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive literalness premise and supplies a relevant genre qualification, though it does not independently verify Petrine dependence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The hyperbole interpretation and its limited purpose—reconciling selectivity with Papias's wording—are clearly stated and stable.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Calling the statement reasonably hyperbolic is proportionate to the general fact that historians and biographers select material.

charity.alternative: Papias's everything may express a substantive completeness claim whose mismatch with Mark counts against the reported Petrine relationship.
charity.decisiveQualification: Ancient universal language can be rhetorical, but genre selectivity alone does not prove that this occurrence is hyperbolic.

logicalCoherence.rationale: Selective biography coherently reconciles omission with nonliteral universal language, with one bounded bridge concerning Papias's intended usage.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The general practice of selective biography supports plausibility, but the excerpt supplies little linguistic or comparative evidence about Papias's exact wording.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary transmission-proximity bridge but addresses a relatively narrow challenge within that tier.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly identifies the literal reading and offers a credible qualification, while leaving text-specific linguistic support compressed.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt quotes the claim that Mark recorded everything remembered from Peter and answers that historians and biographers are selective and Papias spoke hyperbolically.

moves.speaker: Michael Licona
moves.proposition: Synoptic verbal agreement fits traditional authority because Matthew and Luke could use Mark and other reliable written sources, with Greek-language collaborators assisting Matthew.
moves.attributionBasis: The audience question names Licona, and the response states his positions on Markan priority, Q, Matthew’s Aramaic material, and assisted Greek composition.

components.text: Whether extensive Synoptic verbal agreement is incompatible with traditional authority or apostolic proximity.
Whether Greek-language collaborators could mediate Matthew's use of an existing Greek source.
Whether the proposed assistance is historically evidenced at the scale of Gospel composition.

response.rationale: The reply explains how Matthew and Luke could use Mark and other sources while retaining traditional authority, but does not answer the demand for evidence of Gospel-scale assistance.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This partial answer contacts the compatibility challenge and source-use mechanism while leaving the historical-practice warrant materially unanswered.

precisionFindings.rationale: The source-use thesis is clear, but assistance again ranges from translation help to substantive Greek composition without a stable division of labor.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The why-not formulation appropriately establishes compatibility and possibility rather than claiming that source use proves the traditional figures' involvement.

charity.alternative: Anonymous educated authors could use Mark and other sources just as readily, so source dependence may not identify traditional authority.
charity.decisiveQualification: A composition model's compatibility with the data does not make it more probable without discriminating evidence of Matthew's or Luke's involvement.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The source-use account is internally coherent, but the inference from use of reliable sources to named traditional authority remains underdetermined.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Markan borrowing, the additional-material proportion, Luke's preface, and consultation claims are specific, while actual named involvement remains unsupported.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the subsidiary transmission-proximity bridge and ranks high within that tier because it treats both Synoptic source use and assistance.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply explains compatibility well but does not adequately confront the equally compatible anonymous-author alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites Matthew's editing of Mark and additional material, Luke's statement that many had written, and consultation of eyewitnesses or their associates.

moves.speaker: Bart Ehrman
moves.proposition: The possible reliability of Gospel traditions does not identify Matthew or John as authors or authorities, and substantially later attribution cannot substitute for evidence connecting those figures to the texts.
moves.attributionBasis: After confirming the preceding characterization, Ehrman redirects the exchange in first person to his repeated evidential question about Matthew and John.

components.text: Whether source reliability and apostolic proximity answer the motion's distinct demand for identification as Matthew or John.
Whether substantially later attribution can supply the missing connection between reliable traditions and the named traditional figures.
Whether the evidence specifically identifies John rather than supporting general eyewitness proximity.

response.rationale: The reply justifies replacing a reliability-focused inquiry with the motion-preserving identification demand and repeatedly asks what specifically connects Matthew and John to the texts.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly preserves the legitimate issue, explains why reliability is insufficient, and answers the replacement demand by identifying the missing authorial connection.

precisionFindings.rationale: Reliability, author identification, authority, and later attribution are carefully separated, leaving a fully recoverable and appropriately bounded proposition.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The move makes the limited burden claim that reliability does not identify an author and that later claims cannot substitute without a connection.

charity.alternative: Reliable source transmission combined with internal fit and external testimony may cumulatively support Matthew or John even if no single item identifies them.
charity.decisiveQualification: The cumulative case still requires some discriminating bridge from reliable material to each specific named authority.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between content reliability and named authorship is explicit, valid, and directly tied to the motion's completion requirement.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The warrant is mainly conceptual and firmly supported by the identified gap, though the exact chronology of later attribution is only summarized here.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the negative motion bridge by arguing that neither named composition nor authorization has been established despite reliability claims.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly allows that traditions may be reliable while precisely identifying the distinct author-identification burden that remains.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt repeatedly distinguishes reliable Gospel traditions and oral transmission from the separate questions why Matthew and why John, then invokes attribution roughly a century later.
